papers.title: Structural deformations of lipid bilayers around membrane proteins inform oligomerization type
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.24.769041 v1

summary.one_liner: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of monomeric and oligomeric forms of ten channels and transporters in POPC bilayers compare membrane thickness, deformation energy, and lipid packing near protein-protein interfaces to test whether membrane defects encode oligomerization type.
summary.plain: Cell membranes are fatty sheets in which proteins often clump together into groups. This study used computer simulations of ten membrane channels and transporters, alone and in groups, to see how each protein bends and disturbs the surrounding fat layer. The authors report that every protein disturbs the membrane up to about 3 nanometers away, and that proteins which always assemble the same way show larger disturbances at their contact surfaces, which are reduced once they group together.
summary.why: It suggests that the shape of the surrounding membrane may help explain why some proteins form stable complexes and others do not, a question relevant to membrane biology and drug design. The text does not establish how general these findings are beyond the ten systems studied, so this should be read as a computational hypothesis rather than a settled result.
summary.background:
- Biological membranes are double layers of lipids (fat-like molecules) that act as a sheet with its own physical properties.
- Membrane proteins sit inside this sheet and can locally thin, bend, or pack the lipids around them.
- Oligomerization means several copies of a protein joining into one complex.
- Coarse-grained molecular dynamics is a simulation method that groups atoms into larger beads to model slow, large-scale motion over longer times.
- POPC is a common lipid used as a standard model membrane component.
- Membrane thickness, deformation energy, and lipid packing parameter are measures of how strained or disordered the membrane is near a protein.
- Obligatory or structurally monomorphic complexes always assemble in the same arrangement; homologs are related proteins from different species.

papers.abstract: A functional definition of a membrane protein's structure is the three-dimensional arrangement of the polypeptide and the structure of the membrane around it. Biological membranes are composed of self-assembled lipid bilayers, with membrane proteins acting as inclusions that perturb this phase. These inclusions induce long-range changes in membrane structure and create an intrinsic, lipid-mediated driving force for membrane protein association. The question is how much different membrane protein folds shape their surrounding membrane to tune the affinity and specificity of this driving force. To investigate this, we conducted a computational study to evaluate whether different membrane protein oligomers exhibit characteristic membrane defects that indicate specificity in complexation. We performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of monomeric and oligomeric states of ten different channels and transporters in POPC bilayers and evaluated changes in membrane thickness, deformation energy, and lipid packing parameters. We found that all the proteins affect their surrounding membrane up to 3 nm from the protein surface. However, we observed larger defects at oligomeric interfaces for obligatory or structurally monomorphic complexes, suggesting that their oligomerization is partly driven by burial of membrane defects. In contrast, oligomers that adopt different quaternary structures across homologs show weaker perturbations at known binding interfaces, and larger perturbations at lipid-facing surfaces. Nevertheless, all systems show fewer membrane defects upon oligomerization, suggesting an underlying lipid-mediated driving force that each protein fold modulates to tune affinity via membrane-mediated oligomerization.

papers.title: A spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of the post-pneumonectomy lung
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.25.768918 v1

summary.one_liner: A spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of rat lung regeneration after pneumonectomy, combining scRNAseq, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and NICHES-based spatial connectomics to describe three tissue states at Days 3, 7 and 14.
summary.plain: When one lung is surgically removed, the remaining lung must adapt and regrow its tissue. This paper maps how the cells and their chemical messaging change in space and over time in rats during that process. The authors report three different tissue patterns at successive time points, including a transient community at Day 7 marked by signaling the authors describe as fibrosis-mimetic and an apparent growth-related pattern at Day 14.
summary.why: Lung regeneration after pneumonectomy is a tractable model for how mammalian tissue repairs itself in place, which matters for understanding lung injury and scarring. The text does not show clinical implications, and the framework is described as generalizable but its performance against other methods is not detailed in the excerpt provided.
summary.background:
- Pneumonectomy: surgical removal of a whole lung; the remaining lung compensates and regrows tissue.
- Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq): measures which genes are active in each individual cell, used to identify cell types.
- Spatial transcriptomics (Xenium): measures gene activity while keeping each cell's location in the tissue intact.
- Cell-cell signaling / connectomics (NICHES): infers which cells are likely communicating with which neighbors, based on gene activity patterns.
- Mesothelium: the thin protective membrane lining the lung surface.
- Macrophages: immune cells that clear debris and send signals during tissue repair.
- Fibrosis: excessive scar-like tissue buildup; "fibrosis-mimetic" signaling refers to signals resembling those of scarring, not scarring itself.
- Perturbational atlas: a map of tissue changes measured after a deliberate disturbance, across time.

papers.abstract: Perturbational spatial atlases have begun to map regenerative dynamics in a variety of tissues, yet lung remodeling has not been characterized at comparable spatial and temporal resolution. Post-pneumonectomy lung regeneration (PPLR) provides a tractable mammalian model for tissue regeneration that can be studied in situ. Here, we present a spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of PPLR in Rattus norvegicus, combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), high-resolution spatial transcriptomics (10x Genomics Xenium), and NICHES-based spatial tissue connectomics. We observe three distinct tissue architectures at successive timepoints after pneumonectomy, each characterized by coordinated shifts in local cellular composition and intercellular signaling. At Day 3 (D3), a line of interstitial macrophages colocalizes directly beneath an intact mesothelium among active mechanotransductive and inflammatory signaling. We also observe the unexpected appearance of a transitional remodeling cellular community at D7 which appears largely absent at later timepoints, marked by fibrosis- mimetic signaling. At D14, an alveologenic architecture at distal lung tissue displays a connectivity signature consistent with active de novo growth, distinct from baseline homeostasis. Our findings establish a spatiotemporal map of multicellular architecture during regenerative lung remodeling and introduce a generalizable framework for spatial connectomic analysis to be used in perturbational tissue systems biology.

papers.title: NanoHIV-DR: a Nextflow workflow for consensus and read level HIV-1 drug resistance profiling from Oxford Nanopore sequencing
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768148 v1

summary.background:
- HIV-1 drug resistance: viral mutations that reduce how well antiretroviral drugs work.
- Genotyping: reading the viral genetic sequence to look for these mutations.
- Oxford Nanopore sequencing: a portable method that reads long DNA/RNA strands by measuring electrical signal changes as they pass through a pore; raw signal files are POD5 format.
- Basecalling: converting raw signal into letters (A, C, G, T).
- Demultiplexing: sorting pooled reads back to their original samples by barcode.
- Read alignment and consensus: matching reads to a reference genome and summarising them into one sequence.
- Sierra: a tool that interprets resistance from consensus sequences.
- Nextflow: a workflow system for running chained analysis steps reproducibly.
summary.one_liner: NanoHIV-DR is a Nextflow workflow that takes raw Oxford Nanopore HIV-1 sequencing data through basecalling, demultiplexing, host-read removal, filtering, alignment and consensus building, then reports drug-resistance mutations using both consensus-level (Sierra) and read-level analysis.
summary.plain: HIV treatment can fail when the virus carries mutations that make drugs less effective, so labs sequence the virus to check for them. This paper describes a software pipeline that automates the many computing steps needed to turn raw data from a portable DNA-reading device (Oxford Nanopore) into a readable drug-resistance report. The pipeline can also pick up mutations that exist only in a minority of viral copies, which a standard averaged result would miss.
summary.why: Faster, portable sequencing for HIV drug resistance could make testing easier to run in clinics with limited bioinformatics staff, which matters for treatment decisions. The text describes the workflow and its goals but does not report accuracy or validation results, so its practical performance is not yet shown here.

papers.abstract: Oxford Nanopore sequencing offers a rapid and portable approach for HIV-1 drug resistance (HIVDR) genotyping, but analysis of the resulting long-read data requires multiple bioinformatics steps and currently available nanopore workflows are limited. We developed NanoHIV-DR, a Nextflow-based workflow that streamlines the analysis of Oxford Nanopore sequencing data and generation of HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR processes raw POD5 files through basecalling, demultiplexing, host-read removal, quality filtering, read alignment and consensus generation, before identifying resistance-associated mutations and interpreting predicted drug susceptibility. The workflow provides two complementary approaches to HIVDR analysis: consensus-based resistance interpretation using Sierra and read-level detection of resistance-associated variants, enabling mutations below the consensus level to be identified and quantified. Outputs are integrated with clinical metadata to generate human-readable HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR provides a reproducible and accessible workflow for Nanopore-based HIVDR analysis with reduced bioinformatics expertise and manual processing for translating long-read sequencing data into interpretable resistance profiles.

papers.title: GlycoBind: a general toolkit for protein-glycan binding prediction
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.25.769100 v1

summary.background:
- Glycans: chains of sugar molecules attached to proteins and lipids on cell surfaces.
- Protein-glycan binding: a protein physically docking onto a specific sugar chain, a key step in cell signalling and infection.
- Protein Data Bank (PDB) format: the standard file type for 3D protein structures.
- IUPAC-condensed notation: a text string that spells out a glycan's structure.
- Glycan arrays: lab plates printed with many different sugars, used to measure which proteins bind which glycans and how strongly.
- AUROC: a score for how well a model ranks true binders above non-binders; 0.5 is random guessing.
- Frozen representations: pretrained feature encoders (DeepGlycanSite, GlycanGT) whose weights are fixed; only the small final classifier is trained.
- Holdout test: evaluating on proteins or data withheld from training, to check the model generalises.
summary.one_liner: GlycoBind is a computational toolkit that scores how likely a protein structure is to bind an intact IUPAC-named glycan, without needing a solved complex or docking pose, by combining frozen DeepGlycanSite protein features with frozen GlycanGT glycan graph features through a small trainable classifier.
summary.plain: Sugar chains (glycans) decorate proteins and cells and help them recognise one another, for example in immune responses and in how pathogens stick to host tissue. This paper presents GlycoBind, a software tool that takes a protein's 3D structure and a written description of a sugar chain and outputs a score for how strongly they might bind. The authors report a mean AUROC (a 0 to 1 measure of ranking accuracy, where 0.5 is chance) of 0.767 across five holdout tests grouped by protein, and say it ranked binding strength better than existing models on six external glycan-array datasets.
summary.why: Predicting which sugar chains a protein will grab is hard, and lab screening is slow and costly, so a tool that flags likely strong binders could help choose experiments. The text suggests possible uses in studying recognition mechanisms and designing glycan-targeted drugs, but these are stated as possibilities rather than demonstrated results.

papers.abstract: Protein-glycan recognition controls immune responses, host-pathogen adhesion, cell signalling and the functional organization of the glycocalyx. Computational models can predict protein binding to monosaccharides or short oligosaccharides, but predicting binding to structurally diverse intact glycans remains challenging. Here we present GlycoBind, a general toolkit that accepts a protein structure in Protein Data Bank (PDB) format and an International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)-condensed glycan, and returns a binding score without requiring a protein-glycan complex or a docking pose. GlycoBind adopts the frozen residue-state representation of DeepGlycanSite, a carbohydrate-binding-site predictor, and combines this protein representation with frozen GlycanGT graph representations through a compact trainable classifier. Across five protein-grouped holdouts, GlycoBind achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.767. On six external glycan-array datasets after exact protein and glycan cleaning for both models, GlycoBind showed higher aggregate binding-strength ranking performance and stronger recovery of high-intensity binding pairs than the existing models. By prioritizing high-intensity pairs for experimental follow-up, GlycoBind may support mechanistic studies of protein-glycan recognition and the rational development of glycan-targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: Tuning evolutionary information in MSAs shapes protein generation and folding
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.768656 v1

summary.background:
- Multiple sequence alignment (MSA): a table lining up many related protein sequences so that matching positions sit in the same column.
- Homologues: sequences related by shared evolutionary ancestry.
- Information content (bits per site): a measure of how strongly a column is conserved; low values mean the position varies a lot across sequences.
- Structure prediction confidence: the model's own score of how sure it is about a predicted 3D shape.
- Generative protein models: systems that propose new amino acid sequences; "decoder uncertainty" refers to how unsure the generator is when choosing residues.
- Matched-depth control: a comparison set with the same number of sequences but chosen at random, to separate the effect of selection from the effect of size.
- The text is an abstract-level summary; methods and effect sizes are not given, so the findings should be read as preliminary.
summary.one_liner: The paper tests whether changing which homologous sequences are included in a protein multiple sequence alignment (MSA), and thereby its per-site information content, steers generative protein design and structure prediction outcomes.
summary.plain: Researchers who use computer models to design or predict protein shapes feed them a collection of related protein sequences from many species. This study asks whether deliberately choosing which sequences go into that collection, rather than treating the collection as fixed, changes what the models generate and how confidently they predict structures. The authors report that the coherence of the chosen sequences tracked both structure-prediction confidence and how novel the generated sequences were, with the strongest effects near a particular information level.
summary.why: It suggests that the input alignment, often treated as a fixed preprocessing step, is a lever that can change model behaviour, which matters for anyone relying on these tools for design. The text does not show how broadly the effects generalise beyond the 45-protein cohort and the benchmark named, so the scale of the practical impact is unclear.

papers.abstract: Protein multiple sequence alignments are widely regarded as fixed artifacts of homologue retrieval. An alignment's row composition shapes the evolutionary context that is supplied to a protein model. In this study, we tested whether tuning row composition would steer protein generation and structure prediction outcomes. We tuned lower-tail alignment information by controlling row selection within a reference protein-projected coordinate frame. We paired each information-targeted alignment with a matched-depth random-row control alignment. Across a cohort of 45 diverse proteins, row coherence among the retained homologues is predictive of structural confidence readouts and generated sequence novelty. The strongest row-coherence states occur near an empirical lower-tail information reference point of 1 bit/site. Below this reference point, generated de novo sequences demonstrate more eager exploration, higher decoder uncertainty, and reduced structural confidence at mutated positions. Across an independent structure-prediction benchmark, controlling the fraction of low-information positions demonstrated that intermediate fractions of low-information positions were associated with improved structure prediction within a confidence-gated subset. These findings evince that evolutionary information in protein alignments can be tuned to shape protein generation and structure prediction results.

papers.title: Microbiome complexity shapes host transcriptional networks across the ileum-liver axis
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767119 v1

summary.background:
- Microbiome: the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the gut.
- Germ-free mouse: raised with no microbes at all, used as a baseline.
- Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota-12 (MM12): a defined, simplified community of 12 bacterial strains.
- Specific pathogen free (SPF): mice with a normal, diverse microbiome but free of known pathogens.
- Terminal ileum: the last section of the small intestine, where nutrients and bile acids are absorbed.
- Transcriptome: the full set of gene activity readings in a tissue sample.
- Co-expression network: a map of genes whose activity rises and falls together, suggesting shared regulation.
- Gut-liver axis: the two-way communication between the intestine and the liver, partly via bile acids and immune cells.
summary.one_liner: Transcriptomic survey of mouse terminal ileum across germ-free, defined 12-strain microbiota (MM12), and specific-pathogen-free conditions, examining how microbiome complexity shapes co-expression networks linked to the ileum-liver axis.
summary.plain: This paper asks how much the community of microbes living in the gut changes the genes that are switched on in the lower small intestine (the terminal ileum) of mice, and whether that reaches the liver. The researchers compared mice with no microbes (germ-free), mice with a simple set of 12 known bacterial strains, and mice with a normal, diverse microbiome, with 15 animals in each group. The text provided ends at the study design, so the actual findings are not described here.
summary.why: Gut microbes are known to influence the immune system, bile acid handling and liver function, so tracing how their complexity tunes gene activity in the gut could help explain gut-liver links. The available text does not report results, so its significance beyond the stated aim cannot yet be judged.

papers.abstract: The microbiome plays an increasingly recognised role in development, metabolism and immunity across all segments of the small and large intestine, as well as more distant organs such as the liver. In the terminal ileum - a key site of nutrient absorption - the presence of microbes dictates the development of secondary lymphoid structures (Peyers patches), mediates bile acid metabolism, and impacts absorption. In part, coordinated regulatory networks in the gut impact liver function and immunity through gut-liver connectivity and the movement of immune cells and bioactive small molecules that includes bile acids and other bacterial metabolites. We aimed to examine the extent of microbiome involvement in ileal transcription, where subtle changes in co-expression networks can be tuned by microbiome diversity, composition and function. We surveyed ileal transcriptomes across mouse models which vary in microbiome complexity ranging from germ-free (GF, n = 15), the Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota-12 (MM12, n = 15), and specific pathogen free (SPF, n = 15).

papers.title: APEs: Agentic Prediction of Epitopes to Guide Antibody-Antigen Structure Prediction
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.768576 v1

summary.background:
- Antibody: an immune protein that binds a specific target molecule (antigen).
- Epitope: the patch of residues (amino acids) on the antigen that the antibody contacts.
- Antibody-antigen complex: the 3D structure formed when the two proteins bind.
- CASP: a community blind contest in which groups predict protein structures before experimental results are published.
- DockQ: a 0-1 score for how accurately a predicted complex matches the true one.
- ipSAE: a confidence score for interface quality, used here to pick among models.
- Protenix-v1: a structure-prediction model; "sampling" means generating many candidate poses.
- Retrospective evaluation: testing on past targets while restricting searches to information available before each target's release date.
summary.one_liner: APEs is an LLM-agent system that retrieves pre-target public evidence to propose ranked residue-level epitope patches, which are then used to steer Protenix-v1 sampling and select antibody-antigen complex models evaluated on CASP16 and CASP17 targets.
summary.plain: Antibodies stick to specific spots on a target protein, called the epitope, and computer models often struggle to predict where those spots are and how the two proteins fit together. This paper describes a system that searches public sources for clues about the target, uses them to suggest likely contact spots, and then uses those suggestions to guide a structure-prediction model's sampling and choice of final models. On retrospective CASP test targets, the top suggested spot was at least 50% correct for nine of 14 targets, and the best selected models scored higher on average than the unguided top-ranked models.
summary.why: Predicting antibody-antigen structures is a hard, practically important problem for drug and vaccine design, and the paper shows that public, target-specific evidence can be used at inference time to guide predictions. The gains are reported on a small set of targets, and the prospective CASP17 release is still untested in the text, so the broader value is unclear.

papers.abstract: Antibody-antigen complex prediction remains difficult because the surface recognized by a specific antibody is often uncertain, and model confidence may not distinguish alternative poses. We developed APEs (Agentic Prediction of Epitopes for Structure Prediction), an agentic system that retrieves public evidence, interprets predicted antibody and antigen structures, and produces ranked residue-level epitope hypotheses. For retrospective evaluation, web retrieval was restricted to sources released before each CASP target entry date. Across eight CASP16 and six released CASP17 targets, the top-ranked patch reached residue precision of at least 0.5 for nine of 14 targets. We then used the predicted epitopes to steer additional Protenix-v1 sampling and to compare steered finalists with the highest ipSAE unsteered model. The retrospective best selection across three independent router calls increased mean DockQ from 0.306 to 0.375; DockQ increased from 0.089 to 0.679 for H2321 and from 0.005 to 0.379 for H2346. These results show that publicly available evidence specific to the target antibody-antigen complex can serve as an inference-time signal for epitope localization, guided complex sampling, and model selection. We also release predictions for CASP17 targets whose experimental structures had not been released when the predictions were finalized, providing a prospective test of APEs (https://github.com/CSSB-SNU/ape).

papers.title: Koopman Analysis Reveals Collective Modes Governing Cellular Dynamics
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767672 v1

summary.background:
- Nonlinear system: outputs do not scale simply with inputs, so small changes can have large or unexpected effects.
- Linearization: approximating a complicated system with simpler linear rules; most standard versions only work near one reference state.
- Koopman operator: a method that tracks how measurements of a system evolve, allowing a nonlinear system to be described linearly over its whole state space.
- Normal modes: independent patterns of collective motion in a system, familiar from vibrating molecules and crystals.
- Slow manifold: the lower-dimensional set of states that a system settles onto over long times.
- Gene regulatory network: the web of interactions by which genes switch each other on or off.
- Whole-cell model: a computer simulation that represents many cellular processes together.
summary.one_liner: The paper applies Koopman operator theory to whole-cell dynamical models to extract globally defined collective modes, which separate into slow modes forming a low-dimensional manifold and are linked to cell-cycle and cell-state transition processes.
summary.plain: Living cells are very complicated systems whose behavior is hard to predict, especially when they are far from a steady state. This paper uses a mathematical tool called Koopman analysis to re-describe whole-cell computer models in a simpler form, looking for patterns that act across the whole system. The authors report that these patterns relate to specific cell-cycle processes such as mitosis and DNA replication.
summary.why: The approach aims to give a global, rather than only local, simplification of nonlinear biological dynamics, which is a long-standing difficulty. Its value depends on whether the reported links to biology hold up in other models and in experiments; the text alone does not show that.

papers.abstract: Living systems are complex nonlinear systems that operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and this nonlinearity makes their dynamics difficult to analyze. Several linearization techniques have been developed to address this problem, but most are local. Koopman operator theory is a powerful alternative that linearizes a system globally. Here we show that it not only achieves global linearization but also reveals collective modes that govern the dynamics of complex, out-of-equilibrium nonlinear systems. Applying the approach to whole-cell dynamical models, we find that these collective modes have physical and biological significance and relate to distinct processes in the cell cycle and in cell-state transitions. Collective and normal modes are widespread in many-body systems, particularly in condensed matter (e.g., magnons, phonons, hydrodynamic modes) and in macromolecular dynamics (e.g., normal mode analysis). By demonstrating that such modes also exist in cell-state transition dynamics, and in non-equilibrium nonlinear systems more generally, we offer a new theoretical-physics perspective on these systems. The collective modes separate into slow and fast modes. Long-term dynamics are governed by a few dominant slow modes that form a slow manifold of much lower dimension than the original state space. Thus, although the cell is a very high-dimensional system, its cell-cycle dynamics ultimately reduce to a low-dimensional space. Each mode comprises the coordinated behavior of groups of genes and reflects the structure of the underlying gene regulatory network. The modes can also be decomposed into terms that behave like damped harmonic oscillators, drawing an analogy between the modes of a nonlinear system and the normal modes of many-body systems. Finally, our analysis suggests that the dominant modes are closely associated with biological processes in the cell cycle, including mitosis, spindle checkpoint signaling, and DNA replication and repair.

papers.title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768082 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulatory network: a map of which regulatory proteins (transcription factors) control which genes.
- Enhancer: a DNA region that boosts nearby gene activity; many are non-coding.
- CRISPRi (CRISPR interference): a way to switch off specific genes or regions, here paired with single-cell sequencing (Perturb-seq) to read out the effects in each cell.
- ChIP-seq binding priors: lab data showing where a protein physically sits on DNA, used to constrain which links are plausible.
- Co-expression correlation: genes that rise and fall together; often confounded, so it can produce false links.
- AUROC / AUPRC / FDR: standard measures of how well predicted links match held-out truth and how many false positives appear.
- SHAP: a method for explaining which inputs drove a machine-learning model's predictions.
- Survival cohorts (METABRIC, TCGA-BRCA): patient databases used to test whether a gene signature relates to outcome.
summary.one_liner: An interventional gene regulatory network framework combining single-cell CRISPRi Perturb-seq data with ChIP-seq transcription factor binding priors, applied to enhancer loci in MDA-MB-231 triple-negative breast cancer cells, with benchmarking against GENIE3 and co-expression baselines and survival analysis in METABRIC and TCGA-BRCA cohorts.
summary.plain: Cancer cells run on networks of genes switched on and off by regulatory proteins that bind to switch-like DNA regions called enhancers. This paper tries to map those networks by actually switching genes off in cells (using CRISPR interference) and watching what changes, rather than only looking at which genes move up and down together. The authors report that their method predicted which gene-control links were real more accurately than two common comparison methods, and that some proteins, such as MYC and AP-1 family members, appear central to the network.
summary.why: Triple-negative breast cancer has few targeted drug options, so better maps of the control circuits driving it could help point toward candidate targets. The work is computational and the text reports predictions and retrospective associations only; the claimed candidate circuits still require experimental validation, which the authors themselves note is pending.

papers.abstract: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

papers.title: Predicted templates improve the prediction of antibody-antigen structures by AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768078 v1

summary.background:
- Antibody: an immune protein that binds a specific target; its binding site varies a lot between antibodies.
- Antigen: the molecule an antibody binds to.
- Protein structure prediction: using AI or computation to estimate a protein's 3D shape from its sequence.
- AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2: AI models that predict structures of protein complexes.
- Rigid-body docking (PIPER): a traditional method that places two molecular shapes against each other without bending them; it is fast but less accurate.
- Template: a known or approximate structure given to a predictor as a starting guide.
- "Acceptable or better" models: a standard quality grade for predicted protein-protein complexes.
- Random seeds: different starting points for the AI's sampling; running many seeds is expensive.
- Leakage-free benchmark: a test set with no overlap with the data the AI was trained on, so results are not inflated.
summary.one_liner: Adding rigid-body docking-generated templates from PIPER to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2 raises the rate of acceptable antibody-antigen complex predictions on a leakage-free benchmark.
summary.plain: Antibodies are immune proteins that bind to foreign targets (antigens), and computer tools still often fail to predict how the two fit together. This paper tests whether giving AI structure predictors a rough starting "template" of the pair, made by a cheaper traditional docking program called PIPER, helps them find the right shape. The authors report that this raised the share of cases with acceptable top predictions from 56.2% to 63.4% for AlphaFold 3, and that a similar gain appeared with Boltz-2.
summary.why: Antibody-antigen structures matter for drug and vaccine design, and the paper offers a fairly cheap way to improve predictions without massive sampling. The text reports benchmark gains only, so how far these results carry to real-world antibody design is not something it establishes.

papers.abstract: Motivation: In spite of the much improved protein structure prediction methods, the success rate remains low for antibody-antigen complexes. While this can be improved by computationally demanding massive sampling, results are still much poorer than for most other types of protein-protein interactions. In principle, improvement can be achieved by using templates that are close enough to the native structure of the complex, but these are generally not available for antibody-antigen complexes. Results: We explore the use of templates, generated by the computationally inexpensive rigid body docking program PIPER. Applied to a leakage-free antibody-antigen benchmark set, standard AlphaFold 3 with 1000 random seeds yields acceptable or better models as the top predictions for 56.2% of complexes. Adding the PIPER generated templates in the unmasked version of AlphaFold 3 either increases the success rate to 63.4%, or reaches the same 56.2% success rate in about 200 runs. The template-based approach similarly improves antibody-antigen prediction by Boltz-2. This result demonstrates that the space explored by the ML based approach can be expanded by adding templates prepared by traditional docking, compensating for the lack of evolutionary relationship and the limited availability of training data. Availability and Implementation: The ClusPro server (https://cluspro.bu.edu/login.php) containing the PIPER program is free for non-commercial applications and the program is available by request (https://www.vajdalab.org/). All other study data are included in the article and/or supporting information.

papers.title: Macrophage signaling history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses to cytokine stimulation
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.14.765729 v1

summary.background:
- Macrophages: immune cells that engulf microbes and coordinate responses in tissues.
- Cytokines: signaling proteins that cells use to communicate and trigger responses.
- Transcriptional response: changes in which genes a cell switches on or off, measured here as the cell's gene-expression response.
- Interferon-beta (IFN-beta): a cytokine involved in antiviral and antibacterial defense.
- Mycobacterium tuberculosis: the bacterium that causes tuberculosis.
- ESX-1: a secretion system the bacterium uses to inject molecules into host cells; it is a known virulence factor.
- "Plasticity" here means the cell's ability to change its response to new signals.
summary.one_liner: Using primary human macrophages, this paper shows that prior cytokine exposure asymmetrically constrains later transcriptional responses, with IFN-beta acting as a dominant regulator, and that Mycobacterium tuberculosis-induced IFN-beta restricts later cytokine responses in an ESX-1-dependent way.
summary.plain: Immune cells called macrophages receive many chemical signals (cytokines) in sequence, and what they received earlier can change how they react later. This study tested that in human macrophages, showing that the order and identity of earlier signals limit how the cells respond to later ones. It also found that interferon-beta, a signal produced when tuberculosis bacteria infect the cells, restricts later responses, and that this depends on a bacterial secretion system called ESX-1.
summary.why: Infected tissue sees signals arrive one after another, so how earlier signals shape later reactions bears on pathogen clearance and tissue repair. The text does not show clinical consequences, so the link to treatment or disease outcomes remains a question for future work.

papers.abstract: Macrophages perform a wide array of distinct and crucial functions, and therefore tightly regulate their responses to external stimuli. These cells must integrate sequential signals over time to mount an appropriate response to their immunological niche. How prior cytokine stimulation shares macrophage responses to a subsequent stimulus remains poorly understood, yet has important implications for pathogen clearance as well as tissue repair and homeostasis. Here, we systematically characterize transcriptional responses to sequential cytokine stimulation in primary human macrophages, as well as demonstrate the effect of interactions with bacterial pathogens on macrophage transcriptional responses and plasticity. We find that prior stimulation history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses in a stimulus-specific and asymmetric manner. Across the cytokines we tested, we observe that IFN{beta} is a dominant regulator of subsequent responses to other cytokines. We observe that this plasticity restriction is concentration dependent, rapidly established, and persists after cytokine removal. Additionally, we show that endogenous IFN{beta} produced during infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis restricts subsequent cytokine responses in a manner that is dependent on the activity of the bacterial secretion system ESX-1. Taken together, these findings establish a hierarchical model of macrophage responses to cytokines that depends on cytokine identity and order.

papers.title: RADSuite: Improving Species-Level Identification in Microbiome Research
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767742 v1

summary.background:
- 16S rRNA gene: a stable gene found in bacteria and archaea, used as a barcode to identify them.
- Amplicon sequencing: copying and reading just one targeted region of DNA, cheaper than sequencing everything in a sample.
- V regions: variable stretches within the 16S gene; different stretches differ in how well they distinguish species.
- Genus vs. species: a genus is a broader group that can contain several species; species-level resolution is more precise.
- Intragenomic variants: a single bacterial genome can carry several slightly different copies of the 16S gene, which reference databases may not fully capture.
- Metagenomic profiling: estimating which microbes are present in a mixed sample.
summary.one_liner: RADSuite is a toolkit (a curated 16S rRNA gene copy database, RADlib; a variable-region selector, RADx; and an integration guide for metagenomic profilers) aimed at improving species-level identification in 16S amplicon sequencing.
summary.plain: Scientists often identify bacteria by reading a short, standard piece of their genetic code called the 16S gene. This paper describes a set of software tools that work out which parts of that gene can tell closely related bacterial species apart, rather than only their broader genus group. The authors report that their tool can recommend regions that give species-level results for most microbes of interest, even where the commonly used default regions (V3/V4) fall short.
summary.why: Many microbiome studies, in areas from human health to environmental monitoring, can only name bacteria to the genus level, so better species-level naming could sharpen their conclusions. The paper's claims are about the tools' usefulness as a guide for experiment design; the text alone does not show how well they perform in practice against other methods.

papers.abstract: In the last twenty years, the microbiome has become a central focus of biomedical research, with amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene considered the industry standard for taxon identification of prokaryotes due to its cost-effectiveness. However, common target regions in 16S amplicons often do not uniquely distinguish closely related species, restricting many analyses to the genus level. Additionally, curated databases such as NCBI's 16S curated database often do not contain all intragenomic variants of the 16S gene and lack annotation of the 16S genomic composition and gene structure. To address these limitations, our team created RADSuite, a collection of tools which includes a more robust database of 16S gene copies (RADlib), an application that identifies which V regions will allow for species level identification (RADx), and a step-by-step guide for how to integrate RADlib within existing metagenomic profiling software tools. Here we demonstrate the utility of using RADSuite as a guide for designing 16S amplicon sequencing experiments. For example, RADx can be used to recommend 16S components that enable species-level resolution for most microbes of interest, even when industry-standard default amplicon choices (V3/V4) are insufficient. These findings suggest that targeted variable region selection is critical for reliable species identification. As researchers use RADSuite to improve the quality of their experiments, we anticipate improved experimental accuracy in fields of microbiome research from human health to environmental conservation.

papers.title: Gene regulatory networks and the organization of cell differentiation in multicellular organisms
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767571 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulatory network (GRN): a set of genes whose activity switches others on or off; modeled as a diagram of positive (activating) and negative (inhibiting) links.
- Cell differentiation: the process by which a less specialized cell becomes a specialized cell type, such as a skin or nerve cell.
- Hierarchical (tree-like) differentiation: a branching pattern where each step narrows possible cell fates and reversal is rare.
- Dynamic model: a mathematical simulation of how gene activity levels change over time under given inputs.
- Positive feedback cycle: a loop in which genes activate each other, which can lock a cell into a stable state.
- Mutual inhibition: two genes that suppress each other, so only one tends to be active.
- Clonal multicellular organism: an organism that develops from a single cell that divides, such as animals and plants.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses small dynamic gene regulatory network models to identify the network features (positive-feedback cycles and mutual inhibition between cell-type genes) that produce hierarchical, tree-like cell differentiation, and checks these features against published developmental networks.
summary.plain: Cells in a growing animal or plant usually become more specialized in a branching, one-way pattern: a less specialized cell can give rise to two or more specialized types, but specialized cells rarely turn back. The authors asked which simple wiring patterns among genes could produce this pattern, by simulating large numbers of small model networks. They report that only a small minority of such networks behave this way, and that the ones that do share a few recurring features.
summary.why: The work offers a possible explanation for why developmental pathways are so consistently tree-shaped, grounding it in the wiring of gene networks rather than in assumption. The text reports that these features are more common in published experimental developmental networks than chance would predict, and that hierarchy can persist through evolutionary change; how far these model results carry over to real organisms is not established in the text.

papers.abstract: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types. Differentiation pathways arrange into a hierarchical, tree-like organization: regressions from specialized to undifferentiated cell types rarely occur and undifferentiated cell types often have the potential to produce, when subject to distinct stimuli, two or more differently specialized cell types. How cell type transitions acquire such a peculiar disposition requires an explanation that must reside in the properties of gene regulatory networks (GRNs); after all, GRNs orchestrate the changes in gene activity that define cell types. We studied vast numbers of small dynamic model networks to search for elementary GRNs that could yield the simplest hierarchical, developmental-like, differentiation patterns. We found that only a small minority of GRNs are compatible with hierarchical cell type transitions. Importantly, GRNs that yielded developmental-like differentiation patterns shared common traits: One is the presence of tangles of cycles of positive interactions. Genes in such a tangle produce an all-or-none one-way response to a signal. Another such trait is mutual inhibition between genes associated to different specialized cell types, enforcing their mutually exclusive activation. Moreover, these regulatory patterns are more abundant in published experimentally sustained developmental GRNs than as expected by chance. In addition, we show that it is easy to maintain hierarchical cellular differentiation throughout evolution, even when undergoing changes in gene regulatory interactions and developmental mechanisms. Our work supports the prevalence of design principles that organize hierarchically differentiation pathways in clonal multicellular organisms.

papers.title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767577 v1

summary.background:
- RNA is a chain of four bases (A, C, G, U); bases pair with partners to form a folded "secondary structure."
- Structure prediction software estimates the folding from sequence, often combining learned neural scores with thermodynamic energy rules.
- Chemical probing uses reagents that react differently with paired and unpaired bases, giving a reactivity value per nucleotide, but it does not say which base pairs with which.
- Training a model normally needs reference structures; here, probing profiles stand in for part of that supervision.
- Implicit maximum-likelihood estimation is a technique for training models through discrete choices (such as picking a fold) by approximating gradients.
- Exact base-pair prediction means the predicted pairs match the reference pairs precisely.
summary.one_liner: MXfold2, a hybrid neural-thermodynamic RNA folding model, is extended to learn from chemical probing profiles using three training objectives, two of which use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass gradients through discrete folding.
summary.plain: RNA molecules fold into shapes defined by which of their bases pair up, and predicting that shape from the sequence alone usually requires scarce, carefully annotated examples. This paper shows how chemical probing experiments, which measure how reactive each position of an RNA is, can be used as extra training signal. The authors report improved agreement with the chemical measurements and some gains in predicting exact base pairs, in simulations, RNAgym data and external structural tests.
summary.why: Chemical probing data are far more abundant than full structure annotations, so using them could widen the set of RNAs for which sequence-only structure prediction is practical, including RNA families with few known structures. The text does not say how large the gains are or how far they transfer beyond the tested datasets, so the practical reach remains to be judged.

papers.abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

papers.title: Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767212 v1

summary.background:
- Protein structure prediction: AI tools that predict a molecule's 3D shape from its amino acid sequence.
- Antibody-antigen complex: an antibody bound to the molecule it targets (the antigen).
- Co-folding predictor: a model that predicts the shapes of several molecules together, such as an antibody and its target.
- Confidence score: a number a predictor outputs to rate its own answer; the paper's method avoids relying on it.
- DockQ and Success@1: a quality score for how well a predicted binding pose matches the real one, and the share of cases where the top-ranked answer is good enough (DockQ at least 0.49 for medium quality).
- Consensus and sampling: generating many candidate structures and picking those that agree with one another, versus generating many from one model.
- GPU time: the computing cost measured on graphics processors.
summary.one_liner: AbPoolRank is a confidence-free, predictor-agnostic selector that picks the best antibody-antigen complex structure from a mixed pool of outputs from several co-folding predictors, reaching 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 on 103 post-2021 SAbDab2 complexes and beating deep sampling of any single predictor (26-52%).
summary.plain: Antibodies are immune proteins that stick to a target molecule, and predicting the 3D shape of the antibody bound to its target is useful for drug design. This paper argues that instead of running one AI structure predictor many times and trusting its own confidence score, it is better to collect a small set of answers from several different predictors and use a separate scoring method to pick the best one. On 103 recent antibody-target complexes, the mixed pool of 15 structures picked correctly more often than any single predictor sampled 100 times, and it also used less computing time.
summary.why: Choosing the right answer from many AI predictions is a practical bottleneck in structure prediction, and the paper reports both better accuracy and lower compute cost. The text reports results only on the benchmark described; how well it transfers to real drug-discovery workflows is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.

papers.title: Localizing Unsampled Regions in Partially Sampled Pathogen Phylogenies Using Machine Learning
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767590 v1

summary.background:
- A phylogeny is a tree diagram showing how sampled genomes are related by descent; tips are the sampled sequences and branches are the lineages connecting them.
- The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of a group is the earliest point on the tree from which all members of that group descend.
- Machine learning here means a model trained on example trees to predict which branches lead toward missing data.
- Beam search is a method that keeps a small set of the most promising paths while exploring a tree, rather than checking every path.
- Simulated phylogenies are computer-generated trees where the true answer is known, so the method can be scored against it.
- Sampling gaps are common because not every infection is sequenced, so the observed tree can misrepresent the full outbreak.
summary.one_liner: A machine learning and beam-search method that infers, from an observed pathogen phylogeny alone, which branches lead toward unsampled regions and estimates the most recent common ancestor of each missing region, evaluated on simulated and introduced-missingness SARS-CoV-2 trees.
summary.plain: Genetic family trees of viruses are built from the genomes that labs have actually sequenced, but many infections are never sequenced, so some virus lineages may be missing or underrepresented. This paper describes a computer method that looks only at the tree that was built and tries to point to where those gaps are, without seeing any sequences from the missing cases. On 5,000 simulated trees with deliberately removed tips, the best of its candidate locations recovered on average about 90% of the deleted tips.
summary.why: Knowing where sampling is thin could guide where public health teams collect more samples during outbreaks, which matters for spotting new variants. The text reports results only on simulated trees and one SARS-CoV-2 tree with artificially introduced gaps, so its real-world usefulness is not yet shown.

papers.abstract: Motivation: Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results: We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral-descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response.

papers.title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767145 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulatory network (GRN): a map of which genes or regulators control which other genes.
- Single-cell multi-omics: measuring several layers of molecular data (e.g., gene expression and chromatin accessibility) in individual cells.
- Cell-fate transition: a change in which cell type a cell is becoming, such as reprogramming a skin cell toward a stem-like state.
- Graph attention: a neural network technique that weighs connections between nodes (here, genes or regulators) by importance.
- Recurrent memory: a network design that carries information forward across sequential steps, here across time points.
- Validation evidence cited: ChIP-seq (maps where proteins bind DNA), Hi-C (maps 3D genome contacts), and perturbation experiments such as gene knockdown.
- Simulated data: artificial datasets with a known answer, used to test accuracy.
summary.one_liner: DRAFT is a graph attention plus recurrent memory deep learning framework that infers time-varying gene regulatory networks from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics trajectories, validated on simulated data and on mouse reprogramming and Drosophila spermatogenesis datasets.
summary.plain: Cells change their identity over time by switching genes on and off through networks of regulatory control. This paper presents a computer method, called DRAFT, that tries to reconstruct how those control networks rewire as cells move from one fate to another, using data that measure gene activity and chromatin accessibility in the same cells at several time points. The authors report that it performed better than existing methods on simulated data, and that in mouse reprogramming and fruit fly sperm-cell development it recovered interactions supported by outside evidence, including one candidate early regulator, Mondo, whose knockdown changed germline stem cell numbers.
summary.why: Most tools give a single static snapshot of regulation, so a method that tracks how regulation changes over developmental time could help explain cell-fate decisions. The experimental follow-up on Mondo is a concrete test of one prediction, but the text is a draft and gives few details, so the general claims should be treated as provisional until the full paper is available.

papers.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.

papers.title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767325 v1

summary.background:
- Protein complex: several protein chains that assemble into one functional unit.
- Stoichiometry: how many copies of each chain are in the complex (e.g., 2 copies of A and 1 of B).
- AlphaFold3: an AI tool that predicts 3D protein structures from sequences.
- CASP: a biennial blind competition for testing structure prediction methods; CASP17 is a recent round.
- Large language model (LLM) agent: an AI system that plans steps, calls tools or databases, and reasons in text.
- Top-1/top-3/top-5 accuracy: whether the correct answer is the first, or among the first three or five, of the ranked candidates.
- Chain of thought: the written reasoning trail the model produces for its decisions.
summary.one_liner: StoiAgent is an LLM-driven agent that gathers sequence, template, AlphaFold3, and literature evidence to rank candidate subunit copy-number stoichiometries for protein complexes, reporting 75.0% top-1 accuracy on 56 CASP17 targets.
summary.plain: Proteins often work together as multi-part machines, and structure prediction tools need to know how many copies of each part are in the assembly, which is often unknown. This paper describes an AI agent that collects clues from protein sequences, known structures, AI-predicted structures, and scientific papers, then proposes and ranks possible copy-number arrangements while writing out its reasoning. On 56 benchmark targets from the CASP17 competition, it got the top answer right 75.0% of the time, about as well as a comparable method (StoPred) and better than the earlier PreStoi approach with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%).
summary.why: Getting the stoichiometry wrong can make structure models of protein complexes misleading, so a more accurate and explainable way to set this input could help downstream modeling. The text reports only top-1, top-3, and top-5 accuracy on a single benchmark set, so how well it generalizes to other complexes is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.

papers.title: Gene network topologies for heterogeneity restoration during self-renewal
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767011 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulatory network: a set of genes whose activity switches one another on or off, like a wiring diagram.
- Feedback loop: a gene's output loops back to affect its own activity. Positive feedback tends to reinforce a state; negative feedback tends to hold it steady or oscillate.
- Heterogeneity: cells in one population differ from each other in gene activity, even when genetically identical.
- Multimodal expression: when measured across many cells, gene activity clusters into several distinct groups or peaks.
- Stochastic noise: random fluctuations in gene activity inside individual cells.
- Self-renewal: a population's ability to maintain itself while still producing varied cell types.
summary.one_liner: A systematic mathematical study of how gene regulatory network topology, especially feedback loops, can restore a multimodal (heterogeneous) gene expression pattern in a population that started out homogeneous, with implications for stem and cancer cell dynamics.
summary.plain: Cells in a tissue or a tumor often end up with a mix of different gene activity states, even when they began as identical copies. This paper uses computer models of gene activity in single cells and of how populations of cells grow and change to ask which wiring patterns of genes can rebuild that mix from a uniform starting group. The authors report that feedback loops are a key ingredient, and that networks with both positive and negative feedback were the most robust to changes in rates and noise.
summary.why: Keeping a mix of cell types is part of how stem cells maintain tissues and how tumors resist treatment, so knowing which gene circuit designs can rebuild that mix may point to new targets. The text is a modeling study and does not test these predictions experimentally, so its relevance to real cells is still an open question.

papers.abstract: The ability for a subset of cells to establish a heterogeneous cell population with multi-lineage competency is crucial for the self-renewal capacity of tissues and organs. Restoration of heterogeneous gene expression patterns has been observed in pluripotent and multi-potent stem cells, and the heterogeneity restoration can influence the potential of differentiation into multiple cell types. Similarly, cancer cells can acquire the capacity to establish non-genetic heterogeneity that plays a role in cancer progression and resistance to therapeutics. Specific models of gene regulatory networks have been proposed to explain heterogeneity restoration. However, due to the lack of systematic analysis, it is unclear which network topologies are more efficient for this multicellular function, and what intrinsic and extrinsic factors can determine the optimal choice of network topology. In this work, we use mathematical models describing gene expression of single cells and their underlying population dynamics to examine the influence of network topology on the recovery of multimodal expression patterns originating from a homogeneous population. We found that feedback loops are a key factor contributing to heterogeneity restoration. Negative and positive feedback loops support the existence of heterogeneity restoration, but only positive feedback can accelerate the process with low cost of single-cell-level variations of expression. Furthermore, networks with mixed feedback were the most robust ones for heterogeneity restoration with respect to changes in both kinetic rate constants and noise levels. Using experimentally validated network databases, we showed that genes involved in feedback loops are enriched with functions related to cell fate decisions, and we identified examples of realistic gene regulatory networks cell fate dynamics. Our results suggest multiple potential evolutionary paths towards gene circuits governing heterogeneity restoration and key factors contributing to the dynamics of this process. We expect that this systematic study will enable future discoveries of new gene regulatory networks governing progenitor and cancer cell dynamics as well as therapeutic strategies targeting heterogeneity-enabling circuits.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Missense Variant Pathogenicity Prediction in the KCNQ Gene Family
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767028 v1

summary.background:
- Missense variant: a single-letter change in DNA that swaps one amino acid for another in a protein; it may be harmless or disease-causing.
- KCNQ genes: a family of genes that build voltage-gated potassium channels, which help control electrical signaling in nerves and heart muscle.
- Pathogenicity prediction: using computer models trained on labeled examples to estimate whether a variant causes disease.
- Machine learning classifier: a model that learns from labeled data to sort new cases into categories.
- Quantum machine learning: using quantum circuits as part of a learning model; current hardware is small and noisy, so these are often simulated or hybrid with classical computing.
- AUC-ROC: a score from 0 to 1 summarizing how well a classifier ranks positive cases above negative ones; higher is better, 0.5 is chance.
- Quantum advantage: a clear, demonstrated benefit of a quantum method over the best classical ones; the paper says this was not observed.
summary.one_liner: A hybrid quantum machine learning model (data re-uploading quantum neural networks combined with quantum support vector machines) is applied to classifying missense variants as benign or pathogenic across the KCNQ potassium channel gene family, reporting AUC-ROC around 0.94 but no clear quantum advantage over classical methods.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether quantum computing methods can help tell harmless genetic typos from harmful ones in a family of genes that code for potassium channels, which are involved in brain and heart disorders. The authors tested a hybrid quantum-classical model and tuned its circuit design, reporting performance around 0.94 on a common accuracy score that they describe as comparable to or better than standard classical methods. They also state plainly that no clear quantum advantage was observed.
summary.why: Accurate prediction of which variants in these genes are harmful matters for diagnosing neurological and cardiac disease, so the tools are of practical interest. The work is a early exploratory test of quantum machine learning on this task; its value lies mainly in showing the approach is workable, not in a demonstrated improvement over existing tools.

papers.abstract: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.

papers.title: ProtFlap: Structure-based Deep Learning Prediction of Protein Flexibility from Atomic Energy Networks
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766391 v1

summary.background:
- Proteins are chains of amino acids folding into 3D shapes; "residues" are the individual amino acids.
- Flexibility means how much a residue moves or fluctuates over time.
- Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation: computing how atoms move over time using physics equations; accurate but computationally expensive.
- RMSF (root-mean-square fluctuation): a standard measure of how much each residue wiggles around its average position; here normalised so values are comparable.
- Graph neural network: a machine learning model that operates on networks of connected items, here residues linked by spatial proximity.
- Atomic energy / van der Waals terms: estimates of the forces between nearby atoms from a empirical energy function, applied to one minimised snapshot of the structure.
- Feature attribution: a way to measure which inputs most influenced a model's output.
summary.one_liner: ProtFlap is a graph neural network that predicts residue-level flexibility from a single energy-minimised static protein structure, using atomic energy features and RMSF labels from short MD simulations, with van der Waals terms as the main contributors.
summary.plain: Proteins are not rigid; their parts wobble and shift, and that movement often matters for how they bind other molecules or act as catalysts. Computer simulations can capture this movement but are slow, so this paper describes a method that estimates which parts of a protein are likely to be more flexible using only one static 3D structure. The authors report that it predicts relative flexibility across diverse protein domains and that the interaction energies between atoms (especially a weak attractive-repulsive force called van der Waals) contribute most to its predictions.
summary.why: Fast estimates of flexibility could help researchers screen many proteins or add dynamic information to the static structures that AI prediction tools now produce at scale. The text does not report comparisons against other methods or how well it works on proteins unlike its training data, so its practical value is not yet established from this description alone.

papers.abstract: Protein flexibility is a key determinant of molecular recognition, catalysis, and regulation, yet remains difficult to characterise at scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed descriptions of time-dependent dynamics but are computationally expensive. Although recent AI-based structure prediction methods have substantially improved access to high-quality static protein structures, they inherently lack information regarding the dynamic fluctuations essential for functional understanding. There is therefore a need for scalable, structure-based computational approaches that can infer intrinsic protein flexibility without explicit dynamical sampling. We present ProtFlap, a graph neural network framework for predicting relative residue-level flexibility directly from static protein structures. ProtFlap represents proteins as residue interaction graphs and integrates empirical atomic energy features extracted from a single energy-minimised snapshot with structural and sequence-derived descriptors. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that the local atomic energy network encoded in a frozen protein structure contains sufficient information to estimate structural flexibility. Trained using atomic mobility labels, quantified via normalised root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) derived from short MD simulations, ProtFlap achieves robust and accurate flexibility prediction across diverse protein domains. Feature attribution analysis reveals that van der Waals-related energy terms are the dominant contributors to the prediction.

papers.title: MeXalign - A Segmentation Mask-Based Registration Pipeline for Multimodal Single-Cell Analysis
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766144 v1

summary.background:
- Image coregistration: computationally aligning two images of the same sample so that features line up.
- Segmentation mask: a map that outlines each individual cell in an image, here used as a shared, modality-independent description of cell shape and layout.
- Single-cell resolution: analysis at the level of individual cells rather than averaged tissue regions.
- LA-ICP-TOFMS: laser ablation mass spectrometry imaging that maps metal labels and elements in a sample.
- Immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy: imaging that uses fluorescent antibody tags to show specific molecules.
- Consecutive tissue sections: thin slices cut one after another from a sample, which contain similar but not identical cells.
- Cytospin: a prepared slide of cells deposited by centrifugation, used as a simple test sample.
summary.one_liner: MeXalign is a segmentation-mask-based pipeline that coregisters sequentially acquired LA-ICP-TOFMS and immunofluorescence single-cell images from the same specimen, validated on cytospins, murine tumor and human skin samples.
summary.plain: Scientists often image the same tissue or cell sample with different machines, but consecutive slices never hold exactly the same cells, so lining the images up cell by cell is hard. This paper presents MeXalign, a method that uses outlines of individual cells (segmentation masks) as a common shape to align the two images. The authors tested it on two imaging platforms and report that it improves segmentation and keeps nanoparticle distributions at a subcellular level in a cancer-cell example.
summary.why: Matching the same cells across different imaging methods lets researchers combine what each method reveals about a single cell, which matters for studying drug uptake and cell types. The text reports validation on several sample types, but its broader impact beyond these tests is not established here.

papers.abstract: Leveraging the power of multimodal imaging relies on accurate coregistration of yet fundamentally different modalities. Reliable cell-to-cell correspondence is especially challenging as consecutive tissue sections do not necessarily contain identical cells or cellular structures. Here we present MeXalign, a segmentation-mask-based coregistration pipeline designed to integrate multimodal images acquired sequentially from the same specimen at single-cell resolution. Single-cell segmentation masks provide a modality-independent representation of cellular morphology and spatial organization. MeXalign was tested based on the two platforms, laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-TOFMS) and immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy. As a prerequisite, each modality integrates membrane and/or nucleus labels for accurate segmentation. The added value of MeXalign was highlighted for imaging of cell models deposited on glass slides and tissue sections. The performance of coregistration was validated on cytospins, murine tumor and human skin samples. A dedicated scoring system was introduced allowing to assess the quality of image coregistration. The robustness towards under-segmentation and downstream image analysis was evaluated on LA-ICP-TOFMS with and without coregistration, investigating metal drug uptake, barcoding and cellular phenotyping. A showcase study on cancer cells exposed to nanoparticles proved the accuracy, as the nanoparticle distribution was preserved at a subcellular level when using MeXalign. While all examples show the overall improved quality of segmentation, other benefits of complementary labelings can be anticipated, especially for cellular features unique to one modality.
